sections.title: Name and classification
sections.text: The accepted name used here is Inosperma maculatum (Boud.) Matheny & Esteve-Rav., a combination published in 2019. Its basionym is Inocybe maculata Boud. (1885): both names refer to the same taxon, while Inosperma is the genus used in the current classification. The species belongs to the family Inocybaceae.

sections.title: Cap and gills
sections.text: The cap is usually 3–7 cm across (some floras give up to about 8 cm). It begins conical to bell-shaped, then expands while retaining a broad, blunt umbo. Its chestnut to reddish-brown or greyish-brown surface has radial fibrils; the margin may split as it matures. White veil patches or flakes often remain around the umbo, especially on young specimens. The gills are close to fairly close, unequal and adnate; they change from whitish or grey-beige to ochre-brown and have a paler edge.

sections.title: Stem, flesh and odour
sections.text: The fibrous stem is generally 3–8 cm long and 0.8–1.2 cm wide, cylindrical and sometimes slightly bulbous. It is often whitish near the top and base, with a reddish-brown central zone. The flesh is thin, whitish to ochre-yellow. Descriptions report a strong fruity or pleasantly fungal odour; reported variation means odour alone is not a reliable identification character.

sections.title: Habitat and identification
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows on the ground in deciduous woods, including with trees such as beech, and in mixed woodland; European accounts report fruiting mainly in summer and autumn. Soil preferences and frequency vary by region. Brown fibrous caps occur in several Inocybaceae: the white veil remnants, umbo, gills and stem should be considered together, and identification may require microscopic characters.

traits: Conical to bell-shaped cap that expands but retains a broad, blunt umbo; chestnut to reddish-brown, radially fibrillose, with a margin often splitting at maturity
White veil patches or flakes often remain around the umbo, especially on young specimens
Close, unequal and adnate gills, whitish or grey-beige at first then ochre-brown, with a paler edge
Fibrous stem, whitish near both ends and often reddish-brown in the middle, cylindrical and sometimes slightly bulbous; pale flesh
Ectomycorrhizal in deciduous and mixed woodland, reported fruiting mostly in summer and autumn in European accounts
safetyNote: Toxic: the DGfM lists Inosperma maculata among the mushrooms causing muscarine syndrome. Do not eat it. A photograph or this page cannot securely identify a wild mushroom.
